articles.title: China is digging up a 110-metre-high garbage mountain; the 2.55-million-cubic-metre landfill is being turned into new land
articles.summary: China News: A huge mountain of rubbish that once stood 110 metres above Shenzhen is being dug up as China turns a former landfill into valuable urban space. The Y.
articles.body: A huge mountain of rubbish that once stood 110 metres above Shenzhen is being dug up as China turns a former landfill into valuable urban space. The Yulong landfill, which held 2.55 million cubic metres of waste, is now at the centre of the country’s largest landfill excavation project. Workers are removing around 6,000 tonnes of buried waste each day, separating material that can be sent for energy recovery. The operation is expected to free about 300,000 square metres of land for a planned digital industry cluster and ecological green valley. It marks a striking shift in how China is dealing with its ageing waste sites.China is digging up a 110-metre-high garbage mountainThe operation is substantial, with around 6,000 tonnes of buried waste excavated each day. Rather than treating everything removed from the old landfill as useless material, the project separates different types of waste and light combustible materials, including plastics and rubber, can be used for power generation.According to Xinhua, Rao Yiming, an official with Qingshuihe Subdistrict in Luohu District, described the work as more than an environmental clean-up. “This is not just about settling environmental debts, but also about reclaiming space for development,” Rao said. The approach reflects a broader change in how Chinese cities are dealing with older waste sites, particularly as land once considered suitable for dumping has increasingly become surrounded by urban development.More than 80% of Chinese cities have cleaned up old waste sitesChinese cities were once affected by what it called a “garbage siege”, as landfills filled with untreated waste. Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, for example, each produce more than 20,000 tonnes of household waste every day. Yet the role of traditional landfilling has changed sharply, with the four cities now having no landfill that receives untreated household waste.The closure of old landfill sites is also taking place beyond Shenzhen. Xinhua reported that more than 80 per cent of Chinese cities had completed the remediation of aged waste mountains, with landfill capping and ecological restoration becoming mainstream. The Beijing Garden Expo Park was cited as another example, where construction waste, former gravel pits and waste dumps were incorporated into a landscape that was transformed into an ecological park in about three years.China is moving from landfills to waste-to-energyChina’s approach to waste management is also moving towards recovering energy and materials from rubbish rather than simply burying it. Xinhua reported that most household waste is now incinerated, with modern facilities designed to generate electricity, heat and construction materials. In Foshan, Guangdong, an eco-industrial park processes 4,500 tonnes of household waste each day and produces high-temperature steam that is supplied to nearby factories, replacing some fossil-fuel use.The change has been particularly rapid over the past decade. In 2010, China had 119 household waste incineration plants, which handled about 20 per cent of waste, while landfilling remained dominant. By November 2025, incineration accounted for 78.1 per cent of China’s urban household waste treatment capacity, according to official data cited by Xinhua. Modern plants operate furnaces above 850°C, while activated carbon, bag filters and treatment systems are used to control pollutants.China is reclaiming 300,000 square metres of land from wasteThe Yulong project is part of China’s effort to deal with its historic landfill sites. Instead of leaving the 2.55-million-cubic-metre waste deposit beneath a capped surface, workers are excavating the material and processing it as part of a wider restoration project. The aim is to replace the former waste mountain with a new landscape while making the land available for other uses.Once completed, the Shenzhen site is expected to provide around 300,000 square metres of land for a digital industry cluster and ecological green valley. Xinhua presented the project as part of a wider national shift from simply disposing of waste towards recovering resources and restoring land.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lockerbie bombing intended 'to inflict pain and horror', US court told
articles.summary: The US government is arguing that relatives of the victims should be allowed to give evidence during the Libyan suspect's trial.
articles.body:
The bombing of an American airliner over Lockerbie 37 years ago was intended to inflict "pain and horror," a judge has been told.

The US government made the claim as it argued that relatives of the victims should be allowed to give evidence during the trial of a Libyan suspect.

Prosecutors believe their testimony will help the jury understand the impact of the attack, which killed 270 people on December 21, 1988.

They made the request during the latest hearing on the long-delayed case at the District Court for the District of Columbia in Washington DC.

The man facing trial, Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi, was handed over to FBI agents in Libya in 2022 and has been in US custody for nearly four years.

He has denied building and priming the bomb which brought down the plane.

Assistant US attorney Brittany Keil told the court: "The purpose of the plan was to inflict pain and horror that would be reported around the world."

Judge Dabney Friedrich has not ruled on whether relatives of victims should be called as witnesses, but expressed concern that it could cause a high risk of prejudice against Al-Marimi.

Of the 259 passengers and crew who died on the plane , 190 were American, making it the worst terror attack on the US until 9/11.

Another 11 people were killed in Lockerbie when wreckage from the plane destroyed their homes.

After two postponements, Al-Marimi was due to stand trial at the end of last month but the case was called off at the last minute after new evidence came to light.

Judge Friedrich agreed to give the defence more time to consider the fresh information, which has not been made public.

The judge is considering 11 January or 19 January as new dates for the start of jury selection, and made it clear that she would not tolerate further delays.

Now in his mid-70s, Al-Marimi was in court for the hearing and listened impassively to proceedings through an interpreter.

Defence lawyer Laura Koenig said they will need to question new witnesses and present additional expert testimony in response to the new evidence.

The BBC understands that it is alleged to strengthen the prosecution case against Al-Marimi.

Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi confessed to his role in the attack when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012.

He is said to have been involved as part of a plot carried out by the Libyan intelligence service.

His alleged accomplices were Abdelbaset Al-Megrahi and Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah, two Libyan men who stood trial over the bombing 25 years ago.

A Scottish court found Megrahi guilty of mass murder and jailed him for life.

He was freed on compassionate grounds in 2009 after being diagnosed with terminal cancer, and died in Tripoli in 2012.

Fhimah was cleared and returned home to a hero's welcome. He died last month, just days after Al-Marimi's trial was postponed.

articles.title: US redirects $52 million military aid from Europe, Middle East to conversative Latin American nations
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration is redirecting $52 million in US military assistance from four countries in Europe and the Middle East to governments in Cent.
articles.body: The Trump administration is redirecting $52 million in US military assistance from four countries in Europe and the Middle East to governments in Central and South America, as Washington steps up its focus on the Western hemisphere.The state department notified Congress on Tuesday that foreign military financing earmarked for Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia and Iraq would be redirected for Panama, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.The move follows secretary of state Marco Rubio’s visit to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru last week, where he pledged additional US support. The Trump administration has increasingly made the Western hemisphere a priority, particularly in efforts to tackle drug trafficking and illegal immigration.The decision is also the latest in a series of steps that have reduced US financial assistance or troop deployments in Europe. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticised Nato allies over defence spending and other issues.North Macedonia and Slovakia are both members of Nato.At the same time, the administration has strengthened its engagement with right-wing governments across the Americas, as Trump embraces a renewed interpretation of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that asserts US dominance in the region.Foreign military financing allows recipient governments to use US taxpayer funds to buy military equipment from American defence contractors.The state department said the newly redirected funds would be used to “combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal,” arguing that the Western Hemisphere has historically received less US military assistance.“These funds will prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the department said, in an apparent reference to China’s expanding presence in Latin America.While the reallocation does not end US foreign military financing for Tunisia, Iraq, North Macedonia or Slovakia, the state department did not immediately provide details on how much funding would remain available to those countries.The department said the existing allocation of military financing does “not align with the administration’s prioritization of” the Western Hemisphere.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kempton Park killings: South Africa's president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police have not linked the deaths to a serial killer but are investigating this possibility.
articles.body:
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months.

Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked.

"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said.

Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.

"[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said.

One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody.

So far only two of the seven women have been identified.

South Africa calls gender violence a national disaster after protests

I built this 'AI aunt' for women after family tragedy in South Africa

On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her .

President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice."

South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.

The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women.

Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday.

The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days.

On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven.

"After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing.

Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators.

"These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said.

"Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk."

articles.title: Thirteenth Met Police officer sacked after Charing Cross Panorama film
articles.summary: PC Mason O'Connor is dismissed after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, the Met said.
articles.body:
Another Metropolitan Police officer has been dismissed following BBC Panorama's undercover investigation into the force's Charing Cross station.

PC Mason O'Connor was sacked after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, relating to a comment he made to a female colleague, the Met said.

O'Connor was reported to a "proactive wider investigation" following the broadcast of the programme in October 2025 and he has become the 13th officer to be sacked since then, the force added.

Other officers who were covertly filmed for the documentary were seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault.

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was "totally unacceptable".

A disciplinary panel on Tuesday heard that O'Connor had, while off-duty at a pub, told a female colleague that he hoped she would be raped on her way home.

He was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct, the Met said.

As well as the 13 officers the Met has sacked, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said another two men, both former officers, had also been found to have committed gross misconduct.

The policing watchdog added it was still investigating the conduct of a further 15 officers or police staff in the wake of the Panorama film.

"This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated," said the IOPC's Amanda Rowe.

"The sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter," she added.

O'Connor's dismissal comes weeks after his colleague, PC Lloyd Hunter, was also dismissed from the force .

In unaired footage from Panorama which was shared with the IOPC, Hunter was seen saying he enjoyed "Tasering people" and that he hated homeless people.

Met Cmdr Simon Messinger said the pair had been fired for their "appalling comments and attitudes", adding that the force would continue to support the IOPC investigation.

"I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met's determination to improve our culture across the organisation," he said.

articles.title: Can your skin-care routine actually prevent wrinkles? Dermatologists weigh in
articles.summary: You can't stop these telltale signs of aging completely, but the right routine can certainly help slow them down, pros say.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

Wrinkles are coming for us all. And that's not a threat; it's simple biology. As we age, collagen breaks down, skin loses elasticity and nothing we do can rewrite our DNA — or destiny, for that matter. How does that old saying go? The only thing certain in life is wrinkles and taxes, right? (Something like that!)

Still, we don't have to lie back and let life (and the sun) ravage our skin. Sure, there's always Botox and laser treatments, but the right skin care can do a surprising amount. "It is important to remind people that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and it is always better to prevent the lines and sun damage rather than treat it after the fact," explains Dr. Marisa Garshick , a board-certified dermatologist and clinical assistant professor of dermatology at New York Presbyterian-Weill Cornell Medicine. "For someone using sunscreen with a retinoid routinely, they can expect to have less sun spots, less wrinkles and overall healthier-appearing skin as compared to if they did nothing."

The big questions: Which parts of the aging process are actually within your control, and which skin-care ingredients are worth your money? We asked board-certified dermatologists like Garshick to sort it out.

What skin care can (and can't) do for wrinkles

First things first: No cream, serum or elaborate 12-step routine will stop wrinkles from happening. According to Dr. Kseniya Kobets , a board-certified dermatologist based near NYC, signs of aging stem from different sources. "We have intrinsic factors we can't completely control — like genetics, natural aging and metabolic inflammation — and external factors like UV exposure, lifestyle, smoking, diet and exercise," says Kobets. "Skin care is only one piece of that puzzle, but it is an important one."

Garshick puts it just as plainly: "A skin-care routine cannot completely eliminate the potential for lines and wrinkles, given they are also a result of natural aging and genetics," she says. However, it doesn't mean that skin care doesn't help at all. Kobets says a solid routine can help protect existing collagen, support new collagen and slow some visible signs of aging. Garshick agrees, saying that it can "reduce the severity of fine lines and wrinkles over time."

The catch, of course, is that you must be consistent — and have patience. As Garshick explains, skin care can be thought of as an investment in your skin's future. "You may not see a dramatic difference overnight, but staying consistent can lead to benefits in the long term," she explains.

And even though it's never too early to get into skin care (and we're talking an SPF , not retinoids for third-graders), the good news is, it's also never too late to start. Even in your 60s or 70s, you can still protect the collagen and skin you have from additional damage, says Kobets. It's all about using the right stuff.

The best ingredients for preventing wrinkles

Ever wondered what those fancy terms on skin-care labels really mean? Here's what to look for when battling fine lines is your No. 1 priority, from the stuff you know (SPFs) to the stuff you may not (AHAs, PHAs and peptides).

Both derms lead with an all-important SPF. "Sunscreen is considered the No. 1 anti-aging product because it works to prevent signs of skin aging that are associated with cumulative UV exposure, including brown spots, fine lines, wrinkles and skin laxity," says Garshick. Kobets agrees, saying, "If I had to pick one thing, it is still daily sunscreen." She recommends broad-spectrum SPF 30 to 50 and favors mineral sunscreens for sensitive skin and tinted mineral sunscreens for anyone prone to melasma and hyperpigmentation.

Retinoids are next on our experts' lists. "Retinoids remain at the top because we have decades of evidence for improving fine lines, pigmentation and collagen remodeling," says Kobets. While she considers prescription tretinoin "the OG of topical anti-aging," she points out that it's not for everyone. "I recommend over-the-counter retinol and retinal frequently because they can be much easier to tolerate," she says. "The retinoid you actually use consistently is more valuable than the tretinoin sitting in your medicine cabinet because it makes you peel."

Both derms say that other active ingredients, such as vitamin C and acids, are effective but can't replace retinoids. But if your skin is too sensitive for one, using an antioxidant and peptides may be a helpful alternative, Garshick says. "For someone who can tolerate a retinoid, antioxidants and peptides can be used in addition and should be thought of as more complementary rather than a true replacement," she adds. "Antioxidants like vitamin C help neutralize free radical damage generated by environmental stressors, while also supporting collagen and helping address uneven skin tone."

When it comes to AHAs (alpha hydroxy acids) and PHAs (polyhydroxy acids), Kobets says they can "improve dullness, texture and fine lines through exfoliation," and by removing some superficial dead skin cells, they can also help other active ingredients penetrate better. "But exfoliation alone isn't really addressing all of the biology of skin aging," she says.

As for peptides, Garshick points out that different peptides can have different functions, including support for the skin's structure and signaling processes.

"Retinoids, vitamin C, antioxidants and peptides are some of my favorites, but don't underestimate the basics like humectants and barrier-supporting ingredients," says Kobets. She adds that hyaluronic acid, glycerin and ceramides "may not sound as exciting, but hydrated skin looks more plump immediately, and healthy skin is better able to tolerate your higher-impact actives."

The map to a good wrinkle-prevention routine is pretty simple, according to both derms. "It is best to think about these ingredients as a team rather than choosing just one — sunscreen for UV protection, an antioxidant such as vitamin C in the morning and a retinoid and/or peptide at night when appropriate," says Garshick.

Don't overlook affordable moisturizers or sunscreen, Kobets cautions. An affordable brand like CeraVe can "form the backbone of an excellent routine, and you can supplement with the luxury products you love," she says. This moisturizer supports the skin barrier with a powerful trio of ceramides, hyaluronic acid and peptides.

Kobets is a fan of multitasking formulations because "most people don't need six different serums." She says this one is a good example because it combines L-ascorbic acid with peptides and PHA for gentle exfoliation. "You are getting several complementary ingredients in one formulation," she adds.

Medicube products are an affordable way to "to experiment with different formulations and potentially target texture, pigmentation, hydration and overall skin quality," Kobets says. This serum is formulated with PDRN, panthenol, centella asiatica extract and niacinamide to soothe and hydrate the skin while protecting it from the sun. (Another good SPF option from Medicube is No Cast Just Glow , which was No. 1 on our list of the best Korean sunscreens. )

For anyone who is sensitive to retinoids, Garshick says it can help to find an over-the-counter option that also incorporates nourishing ingredients, such as this RoC cream (also a Bethenny Frankel favorite). Along with retinol, it contains glycolic acid, shea butter, squalane and a mineral complex to keep skin firm, smooth and hydrated.

This new serum from Byoma contains a blend of peptides, including the very impressive GHK-Cu , to diffuse existing wrinkles and slow down new ones. It also has vegan PDRN and NMN (a precursor to to NAD+), to support the skin barrier while targeting eight visible signs of aging, including firmness, wrinkle depth, elasticity and hydration.

Another K-beauty option, this face cream is made with PDRN for targeted skin repair sans irritation. Niacinamide, panthenol and hyaluronic acid round it out to soothe skin, reduce redness and support the skin barrier.

Although retinoids are still considered the gold standard topical ingredient for addressing visible signs of aging, many other ingredients can complement a retinoid-based routine, says Garshick. This includes products like this No7 serum, which incorporates glaciology, the brand's peptide and antioxidant blend, along with niacinamide and hyaluronic acid, "which can be used by all skin types and helps to reduce visible skin-aging concerns," she says.

This lightweight moisturizer from Avène is a favorite of Kobets as an over-the-counter retinoid or complementary treatment to prescription tretinoin. It's formulated with 0.05% retinaldehyde to reduce the look of wrinkles and renew and brighten skin with minimal or no irritation.

Another "complementary" suggestion from Garshick is this serum from RescueMD. "Its formula is designed to support the skin's repair processes while also providing hydration and antioxidant support," she says, adding that it "incorporates ingredients like lapachol to help support the skin's natural repair processes and peptides to improve the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles."

articles.title: Meet Samuel Henderson, the 12-year-old who can mimic more than 100 bird calls and is now going viral for his unusual talent
articles.summary: US News: A 12-year-old boy has gained millions of views on social media by copying the calls of more than 100 bird species using only his throat, tongue and ha.
articles.body: A 12-year-old boy has gained millions of views on social media by copying the calls of more than 100 bird species using only his throat, tongue and hands. Samuel Henderson, a middle school student from the United States, began practicing bird calls as a hobby in his family’s garden. Videos of his bird imitations have attracted widespread attention on social media and digital news platforms, including coverage from Yahoo News. His collection of calls includes common backyard birds such as mourning doves, northern cardinals and American robins, as well as birds of prey such as red-tailed hawks, barred owls and bald eagles. Without using whistles or other tools, Henderson copies their pitches, trills and rhythmic calls so accurately that wild birds often respond to him in real time.Early interest and vocal techniqueHenderson’s interest in copying birds grew from his wider love of nature and wildlife. According to reports from Yahoo News, he spent hours listening to recordings of different birds, memorizing their sounds and testing his own voice to match their pitch and tone. Bird sounds are generally divided into two main groups: songs and calls. Songs are often more complex and are mainly used by male birds to mark territory and attract mates. Calls are usually shorter and can be used to warn of danger or keep birds in contact with each other. Henderson learned to copy both by controlling his throat muscles, tongue position and the way he uses his hands to change the amount of air and the tone of his voice.In a video interview featured by Yahoo News, Henderson explained how he learns a new and difficult bird sound. “I listen to the call over and over again until I can hear the different notes in my head,” Henderson said. “Then I try to figure out where in my throat or mouth that sound comes from. Some need a lot of air from the chest, while others are just small clicks with the tongue.”Recognition and social media attentionMany young nature enthusiasts learn to identify birds using books and field guides. Henderson, however, gained wider attention because he can copy bird calls well enough to get real wild birds to respond. His family began sharing short videos of his performances online. The clips show him in forests and gardens calling to wild birds, which often fly to nearby branches and answer him. According to analytics mentioned in Yahoo News broadcasts, the videos have received millions of views across social media and video platforms. The attention has also given Henderson opportunities to perform at local community centers, wildlife conservation events and school assemblies. During these appearances, he uses his talent to teach people about local birds and the importance of protecting their habitats.Scientific context behind bird mimicryHuman bird mimicry depends on controlling the larynx and vocal cords to reproduce sounds that birds make using a different organ. Birds produce their sounds through a specialized vocal organ called the syrinx, which is located at the base of the trachea. The syrinx allows birds to produce two separate sounds at the same time. Humans have a larynx rather than a syrinx, so accurately copying bird calls requires strong breath control and flexible vocal skills. Nature experts cited in regional reports say that while some people can learn simple calls, such as those of bobwhite quail or screech owls, it is extremely unusual for a young amateur to master more than 100 different calls without mechanical tools. Henderson’s collection includes difficult sounds such as the rhythmic hoot of the barred owl and the sharp call of the red-tailed hawk. His ability to quickly move between calls from different species during live performances has earned praise from local birdwatching groups and wildlife educators.Future plans in wildlife conservationDespite his growing popularity online, Henderson remains interested in learning more about wildlife conservation and environmental science. articles.title: Meet Enos Mills, the Kansas teenager who built a cabin near Longs Peak at 15 and helped create Rocky Mountain National Park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At 15, Enos Mills had already built himself a small cabin near Colorado’s Longs Peak. It was an unlikely beginning for someone who would later become .
articles.body: At 15, Enos Mills had already built himself a small cabin near Colorado’s Longs Peak. It was an unlikely beginning for someone who would later become closely associated with the creation of Rocky Mountain National Park. Mills had arrived in Colorado as a sick teenager from Kansas, after doctors warned his parents that he might not live long. Life in the mountains brought a change. He became a guide, writer and keen observer of the wilderness, spending years travelling its trails. But as visitors, miners and loggers put increasing pressure on the landscape, Mills began working towards a different goal: protecting the mountains for the future.The Colorado journey that changed a sick teenager’s lifeEnos Abijah Mills was born on April 22, 1870, on a farm in Kansas. His parents had previously tried their luck as miners in Colorado, although the venture had not provided enough money to keep them there. They returned to Kansas, carrying memories of the mountains with them.Those stories stayed with Mills. He was drawn to the outdoors from an early age, although his childhood was complicated by poor health. Doctors could not determine what was wrong with him, and by the time he was 13, his parents had been warned that he might not live much longer.The family eventually decided that Colorado offered him a better chance. During the 1880s, the state attracted people hoping that its mountain climate would help them recover from illness. For Mills, the move became the beginning of a life almost entirely connected with the outdoors.The teenager who built his own cabin near Longs PeakMoney was tight, so Mills travelled from Kansas to Estes Park by hitchhiking. He found work with relatives who ran a lodge, doing cleaning and other jobs. Away from the building, he began spending long periods on the trails.His health improved, and his familiarity with the surrounding country grew. Before long, he was working as a nature guide. Mills also had a practical goal. He wanted land of his own. During summer he guided visitors in Colorado, while winters were spent in Montana, where he worked as a runner at a mine. The job involved carrying tools and supplies to miners.The money he saved allowed him to purchase a small parcel near Longs Peak. He built a cabin there when he was just 15. Longs Peak became central to his life. Mills climbed it 297 times, according to records held by the Denver Public Library.Mills turns an unconventional education into a life of travelMills never attended school in the usual sense, but that did not stop him from educating himself. Libraries became an important part of his learning, and his interests extended well beyond the mountains.His work in mining provides one example of his ability to teach himself. He eventually became an engineer at the mine, despite working alongside people who had received formal college training.That career ended when a fire destroyed the mine when Mills was 20. He had saved enough money from his jobs to travel, and he set out across the United States, Canada and Europe. He also reached Alaska, at a time when it had not yet become a US state.Mills preferred wilderness to conventional sightseeing. He travelled with a camping mindset, often alone, and began turning his experiences into stories.A meeting with John MuirDuring a period of camping in California, Mills met the naturalist and conservationist John Muir. The two became friends, and Muir encouraged Mills to use his writing as a way of communicating the value of wild places to people who might never see them for themselves.The encounter helped shape the direction of Mills' life. He returned to the Rocky Mountains and continued writing about the landscape. He was also employed by the US government to measure snowfall in the Rockies, a task that required him to spend extended periods alone in remote mountain country. For Mills, isolation provided time to write. His articles began appearing in magazines and attracted readers far beyond Colorado. People living in cities could encounter the mountains through his descriptions even if they had never travelled there.Turning a lodge into a base for visitorsMills eventually purchased the lodge where he had once worked. He renamed it Longs Peak Inn, linking it to the mountain that had become so important to him. The inn gave him another way to introduce people to the Rockies. He guided visitors during the day and spoke about nature in the evenings. His lectures became popular enough that he travelled around the United States to speak about the mountains.There was a tension in this work, though. Mills wanted people to experience the wilderness, but increased visitation also brought problems.When visitors began damaging the landscapeAs tourism increased around the Rockies, Mills saw signs of careless behaviour. Wildflowers were being pulled from the ground, while mining and logging were altering the landscape on a much larger scale. He responded in a fairly direct way. Signs were placed around Estes Park asking visitors to protect wildflowers, including a reminder that flowers should be cut rather than pulled up by their roots.The small notices reflected a much bigger concern. Mills believed that simply encouraging people to appreciate nature would not be enough if the landscape remained vulnerable to development and extraction. He began advocating for a protected area in the Rocky Mountains.The campaign for a national parkMills had already seen what national-park protection could achieve through the work of John Muir in California. Yosemite had become a national park, providing a model for protecting important mountain landscapes. Mills spent years making the case for similar protection in Colorado. He spoke publicly, wrote about the Rockies and tried to persuade government officials and business interests that a national park would benefit the region while safeguarding its natural features.Muir died in 1914, before the campaign reached its conclusion. Mills continued. In January 1915, Congress and President Woodrow Wilson established Rocky Mountain National Park. Mills' long campaign had reached the outcome for which he had been working, and he subsequently became closely associated with the title "Father of Rocky Mountain National Park".Conservation became part of his public workThe creation of the park did not mark the end of Mills' work. He continued travelling and lecturing about forests, wildlife and the value of spending time in natural landscapes. One surviving handbill advertises a 1909 lecture by Mills at Carnegie Hall in New York City. The subject was "Our Friends, The Trees", an indication of how far his public speaking had taken him from the Colorado mountains where his career had begun.His approach to conservation was closely tied to personal experience. Mills had spent years walking trails, camping in remote areas and guiding visitors. He was not simply writing about a distant landscape. Much of his work came from years spent living within it.A family continued the workMills married Esther Burnell in 1918. She also had a place in the history of nature guiding, later becoming the first person to be formally named a professional nature guide by the National Park Service. The couple had one daughter, Enda.Mills' final years were cut short after an accident in New York City in 1922. He had travelled there to give a lecture about Rocky Mountain National Park when he was badly injured in a subway accident. He continued working afterwards but did not fully recover.He died on September 22, 1922, aged 52. Esther and Enda continued making his writings available and carrying on his message about the natural world. Later generations of the family remained connected with his legacy through the Enos Mills Museum in Estes Park.The landscape that first drew Mills to Colorado is now part of a national park visited by thousands of people. Its existence is tied to legislation, government action and wider conservation movements, but Mills' role was unusual. He spent years trying to persuade people that protecting the mountains was worth doing before such protection became official policy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Omar praises India’s foreign policy over Brics mention of Pahalgam, slams Centre on UCC
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: The condemnation of Pahalgam terror attack in the Brics declaration earned praise for India’s foreign policy from Jammu & Kashmir chief .
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The condemnation of Pahalgam terror attack in the Brics declaration earned praise for India’s foreign policy from Jammu & Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah on Tuesday, but the National Conference vice-president hit out at the Centre over what he called an attempt to bring in the Uniform Civil Code through the back door.“The fact that Pahalgam was condemned (at the Brics summit) is significant. Consider how many allies of Pakistan were present in that room. Therefore, for Pahalgam to be mentioned by name, that in itself is a success of our foreign policy,” Omar said while talking to reporters in Srinagar.About China praising India’s foreign policy, he said India should not “seek certificates of approval from other countries”. “The danger with this approach is that tomorrow, if China says something critical about our foreign policy, what will we do then? ... We cannot cherry-pick,” he said.On reports that China had scaled back troops along the Line of Actual Control, he said “...anything that reduces tension along the LoC or the LAC is a positive step”.The J&K CM, however, was critical of the central govt for trying to implement the UCC in all NDA-governed states. “Something of this nature should not be decided by individual states; it has to be decided by the country as a whole,” he said, adding that the Centre should introduce a bill in Parliament instead of trying to bring in UCC through the back door.Accusing the Modi govt of bypassing Parliament, Omar said, “If they have the numbers, they should bring the UCC bill to Parliament. Why are they doing it through individual states?”The remarks came in the backdrop of Union home minister Amit Shah’s statement on Sunday that the UCC will be implemented in all 21 BJP-NDA states before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.Omar pointed out that NDA partners like TDP, JD(U) and LJP (RV) had chosen to be circumspect about the idea. “Given that even some of their own allies do not support it, I do not think they will be able to get it (UCC bill) passed in Parliament. articles.title: Ulverston Turner Prize winner's new vision for hometown
articles.summary: Keith Tyson said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement.
articles.body:
A Turner Prize-winning artist has revealed plans to transform a former car showroom near where he grew up, into a centre for art and learning.

Keith Tyson has bought the former Mercedes-Benz garage on Princes Street in Ulverston, where he said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement.

The privately funded project aims to give young people opportunities to experience art after Tyson's own artistic education was shaped by local libraries growing up.

He said "there were no galleries for miles around" so he thought this could be a chance to "give young people in the community an opportunity to see and learn about art" in a way that he never had.

Tyson said the project was still in its early stages but he was "excited by the building's potential to become an arts destination" for the north.

The artist, who won the Turner Prize in 2002, said he hoped the centre would include exhibition space, a reference library and programmes for schools and the wider community.

"We're still in the very early stages of the project, but I'm really excited about this beautiful building's potential to become an arts destination, celebrating creativity, especially in the north, and supporting learning and engagement through exhibitions, education, and other resources," he said.

Among those pleased to see the plans come forward is Adrian Newnham, Tyson's former art teacher at George Romney School in Dalton.

Newnham said: "I was Keith's art teacher when he was 10-years-old. I told him he had a talent and I kept his artwork.

"When he won the Turner Prize I showed him the artwork I'd kept. He thanked me in the programme when he won. He was a highly talented lad."

Newham said Ulverston already had a strong cultural identity and believed the project could strengthen it further.

"Ulverston is a festival town with a cultural buzz. Hopefully, his venture will raise the artistic status of the town even more," he added.

Tyson became known for work combining art, science and technology across a range of media, including painting, sculpture and installation.

articles.title: A metal detectorist uncovered 4.5 kg of Viking-era silver in Finland; thousands of coins were buried in two birch-bark containers
articles.summary: Europe News: A metal detector enthusiast has uncovered Finland’s largest known Viking-era silver hoard in Sysmä, with thousands of coins and other silver objects f.
articles.body: A metal detector enthusiast has uncovered Finland’s largest known Viking-era silver hoard in Sysmä, with thousands of coins and other silver objects found buried at the site. Kalle Lappinen discovered on 3 September after his detector picked up an unusually large number of signals. The hoard contains around 4.5 kilograms of silver and was buried in two birch-bark containers placed about 12 metres apart, just under half a metre below the ground between stones. The coins have not yet been cleaned or separated, so their exact number and weight are still unknown. Researchers will also need to determine their precise age. Yle (Finland's national public broadcasting company) reports that the discovery is Finland’s largest known late Iron Age coin hoard.How did a metal detectorist uncover Finland’s largest Viking-era silver hoardKalle Lappinen discovered the hoard while metal detecting in Sysmä on 3 September. Thousands of silver coins were found on the site, making the discovery Finland’s largest known Viking-era silver hoard. Archaeologist Esko Tikkala of the Lahti City Museums examined the discovery the following day. The museum described it as Finland’s largest known Late Iron Age coin hoard. It also included a silver bracelet and other silver objects. The silver weighs about 4.5 kilograms. The coins have not been cleaned or separated. Their exact number and weight will be confirmed later, while research will also establish the hoard’s precise age.Thousands of coins were buried in two birch-bark containersThe silver was found in two separate deposits rather than scattered through the soil. The objects had been placed in containers made from birch bark and buried between stones, just under half a metre below the ground. The two containers were about 12 metres apart. They held thousands of silver coins, along with a bracelet and other silver objects. Together, the silver weighs around 4.5 kilograms. However, the exact number of coins is not yet known because they have not been cleaned or separated. Further examination will establish their precise number and weight, which gives researchers a clearer picture of the scale of the hoard.What makes the Sysmä discovery larger than Finland’s previous Viking-era hoardThe discovery is significant because it is the largest known coin hoard from Finland dating to the Late Iron Age. Before the Sysmä find, the largest known Viking-era coin hoard came from Nousiainen. That earlier hoard weighed just over two kilograms and contained around 1,700 coins. The new hoard is heavier, although its exact coin count is still unknown. The comparison shows why the Sysmä discovery is important. Its silver weight has surpassed the previous record. Once the coins are cleaned and separated, researchers will determine the number of pieces.What made the signals from Lappinen’s metal detector so surprisingThe discovery began when Lappinen’s metal detector picked up a large number of signals. He initially found it hard to believe what he was seeing because most signals turn out to be rubbish or metal deposits. Lappinen estimates that about 99% of his finds fall into these categories. This time, however, the signals led him to thousands of silver coins, a bracelet and other silver objects. The finding has been identified as Finland’s largest known Late Iron Age coin hoard and its largest known Viking-era silver hoard. The two birch-bark containers also add to the discovery. Researchers will now examine the coins and other objects to determine more about the hoard.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Scientists discovered an unnamed female mummy in 1935, the Egyptian Mummy has been left screaming for 3,000 years
articles.summary: Tech News News: An ancient Egyptian mummy discovered in Thebes in 1935 has left scientists trying to explain one unusual detail for decades: her face appears frozen i.
articles.body: An ancient Egyptian mummy discovered in Thebes in 1935 has left scientists trying to explain one unusual detail for decades: her face appears frozen in a scream. The woman was buried about 3,000 years ago and had received an expensive burial treatment, making it unlikely that her strange expression was simply the result of poor mummification. As stated in reports, researchers examined the mummy again in 2024 using X-rays, CT scans and several laboratory techniques. They found no clear cause of death, but suggested that a severe and sudden event may have caused a phenomenon known as a cadaveric spasm, leaving the woman’s mouth open and her face contorted at the time of death.3,000-year-old Egyptian mummy discovered in ThebesThe unnamed woman was discovered in 1935 in Thebes, an ancient Egyptian city. Her coffin carried no inscription identifying her. Her appearance immediately drew attention because her mouth was open and her face looked as though she had died while screaming.At first, researchers considered whether poor embalming could have caused the expression. Ancient Egyptian embalmers normally took extensive steps to preserve a body and make it look as natural as possible.However, evidence from the woman’s burial suggested that her body had received careful and costly treatment.Expensive materials used in the mummy's burialThe mummy wore an elaborate wig made from date palm fibres. It had been dyed with reddish henna and covered with a crystalline powder containing quartz, magnetite and albite. Her body, clothing and wig were also treated with imported resins. One of the materials used was frankincense associated with Punt, a region known for exporting valuable goods including aromatic resins and gold. Juniper resin was also used.These details suggested that the woman came from a wealthy section of ancient Egyptian society and that her embalmers had not simply carried out a careless or incomplete mummification.Why was the ancient Egyptian mummy left screamingOne unusual detail remains difficult to explain: the woman’s internal organs were still inside her body. In many ancient Egyptian burials, organs were removed during the mummification process and preserved separately in canopic jars. However, the researchers noted that later embalming practices could sometimes involve drying the organs and returning them to the body. There was no visible incision showing that the organs had been removed.Her arms also provide a clue about her status. They were positioned at her sides and only partly met over her lap. The researchers said this suggests she was not a member of the royal family, as royal mummies were buried with their arms crossed over their chests.Scientists examine the 'screaming woman' mummyIn 2024, mummy radiologist Sahar Saleem of Cairo University and Samia El-Merghani of Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities examined the mummy using several non-destructive methods. The investigation included X-rays and CT scans, as well as scanning electron microscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction analysis.The researchers found that the woman was around 5 feet tall and died at about 48 years old. Signs of wear were visible in her teeth and joints. But the tests did not reveal a clear cause of death.The researchers suggested that the woman's unusual facial position may have been caused by a cadaveric spasm. This phenomenon can involve certain muscles becoming fixed at the moment of death, particularly in cases involving severe pain or panic. It is different from normal rigor mortis because it can affect specific muscles rather than the entire body.The researchers said the expression could indicate that the woman died in extreme pain.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.summary: Carnegie Mellon says Uju Anya's social media posts violated community standards, as colleagues report fearing for their safety after being doxxed.
articles.body: Carnegie Mellon University said Monday it is taking "swift action" after determining that professor Uju Anya’s recent social media posts violated university community standards, with some of her colleagues reporting that they now fear for their personal safety. President Farnam Jahanian and Provost James H. Garrett Jr. said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital that Anya used "expletives, racial slurs and derogatory language that demeaned, dehumanized and intimidated," while using her Carnegie Mellon affiliation and implying support from university colleagues. "Carnegie Mellon University is a place where rigorous inquiry, freedom of expression and mutual respect must coexist," their statement read. "We take that responsibility seriously, and we strongly reject language that is hateful and disparages or calls for the harm of others. Such rhetoric is inconsistent with the dignity, respect and responsibility that we expect from one another." "Dr. Anya’s choice of language violates our shared community standards and distracts from the seriousness and significance of CMU’s scholarship in the humanities and social sciences," the statement added. articles.body: In 2010, an investor bought Bel-Air founder Alphonzo Bell's 1928 estate for $5.5 million; after a five-year restoration, the 10,600-sq-ft mansion is asking $32.5 millionA 1928 mansion that Bel-Air's founder built for himself has hit the market, with an asking price of $32.5 million. The sale comes after a comprehensive five-year restoration, according to a report by Platinum Tribune.The current owner, Michael Wexler, bought the estate for $5.5 million eleven years ago. The 10,600-sq-ft Spanish-style estate is on one of Bel-Air's most coveted perches, with a lineage tracing back to the neighbourhood's founder himself. Wexler had no plans to flip the property when he bought it. He bought it to live in, and he did, for roughly a decade before deciding the house deserved something more ambitious: a complete resurrection. After that, the estate at 10772 Chalon Road was rebranded as Maison de La Reine, and this month it hit the market, asking $32.5 million.Landmark estateReal estate developer and oilman Alphonzo Bell, who established the surrounding neighbourhood and the Bel-Air Country Club, built this mansion in 1928 for himself. Bell went to architect Mark Daniels, the same man who helped him create Bel-Air itself. By then, Daniels had laid out the neighbourhood's streets and planted thousands of trees to frame them. He'd engineered underground equestrian tunnels so riders could navigate the hills without mixing with automobile traffic. This house was Daniels applying that same precision and vision to a single residence.The Spanish-style design reflected 1920s LA, when Mediterranean-inspired homes were a symbol of luxury and fashion. The craftsmanship of the mansion spoke for itself. The house features built-in millwork, hand-carved stone fireplaces, and terrazzo floors laid by hand.The renovationOver the years, the 1928 mansion has had many famous owners, including Queen Noor of Jordan and the late film producer Steven Reuther, who built a private cinema and editing suite on site.In 2010, Maple Leaf Capital CEO Michael Wexler purchased the property for $5.5 million. He lived there for a decade before renovating it in 2021. Rather than gut-renovate, he asked designers Kendra Sosothikul and Paula Press of Studio Berosso to approach the project with a scholar's attention to detail. The original 1928 checkerboard terrazzo foyer was preserved and restored in place. The hand-painted Gracie wallpaper adorning the breakfast room ceiling was either conserved or recreated to match period specifications. He also added some modern flair: custom Gucci wallpaper now lines the private office and theatre powder room, while a Calacatta Viola marble fireplace anchors the formal living room. A new wine cellar was built with hand-laid mosaic flooring. The original indoor pool was reimagined as a climate-controlled fitness space. The outdoor terraces were expanded to frame views towards Century City and Downtown Los Angeles. These upgrades only added a contemporary flair to the historic estate. Listing agent Chris Soffer of The Beverly Hills Estates described the renovation as a continuation of the home's historic character. They managed to find a balance between comfort and history.Chris Soffer holds the listing alongside Trenton Armitage, Rayni Williams, and Branden Williams. The asking price is $32.5 million. The buyer will also have to pay a special 5.5% transfer tax under Los Angeles' Measure ULA. This tax applies to property sales above $10.9 million. For a $32.5 million sale, that would be about $1.78 million in additional tax at the time of the sale.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Israel lacking respect for dead buried in Gaza rubble: UN
articles.summary: Human rights chief reiterates concern over war crimes evidence as remains from entire families are unearthed.
articles.body:
Areas in war-devastated Gaza continue to be razed by Israeli bulldozers with “no respect for the dead”, the United Nations’ human rights chief has said.

Volker Turk criticised Israel’s actions in clearing rubble in the enclave in a statement issued on Tuesday. His words come as the discovery of “extensive” remains have heightened concerns that evidence of war crimes is being destroyed or concealed.

“Much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives,” he said, warning that areas where the Israeli military remains deployed “continue to be levelled by bulldozers with no respect for the dead under the rubble”.

The UN human rights chief said the remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites that were destroyed during Israeli attacks, adding that many victims were women and children.

“It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst ⁠fears confirmed,” he said.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has generated about 61 million tonnes of wreckage and debris. It could take seven years to clear the debris, the UN has estimated.

A US-brokered “ceasefire” in October 2025 has failed to halt regular Israeli strikes and attacks, with more than 1,300 Palestinians killed since the “truce” came into effect, according to Gaza officials.

Palestinian Civil Defence says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.

Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the wreckage.

Turk said he feared the remains recovered ⁠so far could be “only the tip of the iceberg,” noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened ⁠by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.

The UN official also reiterated his concerns over Israel’s conduct , including its extensive use of explosive weapons in densely populated areas, which he said failed to effectively distinguish between civilians and fighters.

“The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces these concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes,” he added.

“The reported killing of large numbers of family members, including children, women and persons with disabilities, in attacks on residential buildings, raises grave concerns regarding compliance with the rules governing the conduct of hostilities,” he said.

On September 6, Palestinians in northern Gaza held funerals for about 100 people , including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings.

Despite last year’s agreement to halt the hostilities, the Israeli military continues its operations in Gaza.

One Palestinian was killed by sniper fire in the north of the enclave on Tuesday.

The man was in the Jabalia refugee camp when he was shot by a sniper positioned on a high-rise crane, Al Jazeera reporters said.

At least two other people were killed in an Israeli drone attack on an industrial area of Gaza City, according to a source from the enclave’s Ambulance and Emergencies service.

articles.title: Data breach relates to Southport attack victims, survivors and families
articles.summary: The Ministry of Justice says sensitive and personal data was accessed in a limited number of cases.
articles.body:
An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said.

The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected.

An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told.

The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Those affected are being notified directly, the department said.

An MOJ spokesperson said: "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families.

"We apologise to those affected - unauthorised access to court files is completely unacceptable.

"This is now being investigated urgently, and the prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this.

"All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action."

The department said it was also reviewing policies and frameworks covering staff conduct, acceptable use and its fraud response plan.

HM Courts and Tribunals Service and HM Prison and Probation Service are also investigating.

Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, were murdered during the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport on 29 July 2024.

The data breach disclosure follows separate cases involving inappropriate or potentially inappropriate access to the medical records of people involved in the attack.

articles.title: Romanian shepards and farmers clash with police
articles.summary: Dozens injured as 2,000 farmers – backed by far-right groups – protest the extension of a livestock export ban.
articles.body:
Riot police have clashed with Romanian shepherds and farmers as they rioted during a protest against a ban on livestock exports due to disease.

About 2,000 people gathered to demonstrate in the capital, Bucharest, on Tuesday against the extension of a live sheep export ban, imposed by the European Union due to the highly contagious small ruminant plague. As in other protests by farmers across Europe in recent years, the rally was encouraged and supported by far-right forces.

Violence broke out in front of the Romanian government building in Bucharest when some protesters demanding the reversal of the ban began throwing rocks, metal barriers and other objects at law enforcement.

Police responded with tear gas in a bid to disperse them. Twenty-six people were detained, riot police said in a press release.

Twenty-four demonstrators and police officers required medical attention – some for broken bones, others for the effects of the tear gas. Four were hospitalised.

The government and the opposition called on the demonstrators to refrain from violence.

The demonstration was called by farmers and shepherd groups. Protesters held banners calling on the country’s president and prime minister to resign.

Some chanted the name of far-right politician Calin Georgescu, a former presidential candidate who is standing trial for acts against the constitutional order following the annulment of the presidential elections in 2024.

Supporters of Georgescu had shared messages on social media ahead of the protest, asking people to join.

George Simion, the leader of the main far-right group in the country, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), wrote on Facebook that “AUR stands with the farmers and all working Romanians”, but called on protesters to demonstrate peacefully.

The Romanian government said in a press release that the protest had “degenerated into regrettable acts of violence” and called for “calm”.

President Nicusor Dan condemned the “extremely serious” violence and “any attempt to turn a legitimate protest into street fighting” in a social media post.

Romanian shepherds had protested outside the government building at the end of July over the EU ban on live sheep exports, which expires at the end of 2026.

The country of 19 million people has been struggling for months with the highest inflation in the EU and a political crisis with no end in sight.

The pro-European government, which adopted austerity measures to rein in a high budget deficit, was brought down in a no-confidence motion in May, and a divided parliament has failed to confirm a successor.

articles.title: Ciara Miller makes her ‘Dancing with the Stars’ debut — these essentials are getting her through long rehearsals and live shows
articles.summary: Summer House star Ciara Miller is competing on Dancing with the Stars season 35. These are her rehearsal, recovery and performance essentials from Nexxus, Bala and more.
articles.body: Talking Shop is our series where we talk to interesting people about their most interesting buys. She took the Hamptons by storm from the moment she joined the cast of Bravo’s Summer House. She held down the fort in Fiji while hosting Love Island: Aftersun. She modeled in campaigns for some of the biggest brands in the world. And now, Ciara Miller is tackling a new challenge: competing for the Mirrorball Trophy on season 35 of Dancing with the Stars, which premiers tonight at 8 p.m. ET on ABC/Disney+. “I’m definitely getting a run for my money,” says Miller, who told me that she’s wanted to do the show for years. “It’s such an experience for growth. I danced growing up, but I did ballet and hip hop and jazz and stuff. This is such a different sector of dance that I wanted to experience.” Miller’s partner this season is Brandon Armstrong, a multi-season DWTS pro. She says he’s been a great teacher and choreographer, but she’s putting her mark on performances, too. “Brandon is in charge of one thing: the dancing,” says Miller. “I’m in charge of everything else. We have creative calls where we can be as involved or not involved as we want, and I’m involved, even down to his outfits.” Before Miller’s first live performance, I talked to her about what she’s using to recover after hours-long rehearsals and products she swears by on the dance floor. And, of course, because she’s the first Summer House cast member to be in the ballroom, I had to ask: If she could cast any of her other housemates on Dancing with the Stars, who would it be? “Kyle [Cooke] would be number one on my Mount Rushmore,” says Miller. “I tried to teach him a pose, and I would really enjoy seeing Kyle attempting to learn any type of dance at all.” Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. One of the most useful purchases Miller has made during Dancing with the Stars rehearsals so far is Bala Bangles. “I just got these arm weights because a lot of my moves this first week are in frame, and my arms look like chicken wings instead of an elegant bird,” she says. “So I was like, okay, what can keep me mindful of keeping my arms up? These weights are how I’ve been training my arms.” She got a pink pair and tries to keep them on for the entirety of each practice session. Miller isn’t shy about sharing what the hardest part about being on Dancing with the Stars is: “I am not flexible anymore, so I really have to stretch,” she says. “My back, my neck… I’m so sore everywhere.” She’s taking recovery very seriously, starting with hot baths. “I’m soaking in a bathtub almost every day for at least 20 minutes. It’s essential,” says Miller. “I’m living for Dr. Teal’s epsom salt. I’ve got the sleepytime one, I’ve got the one for muscle recovery; I’ve got all the things.” To continue winding down after her bath, Miller puts on her favorite red light therapy mask from Currentbody. “It’s flexible, so it can fit into small spaces, and I didn’t have to worry about crushing it when I was traveling, which was nice,” she says, referring to her recent move from New York City to Los Angeles. “I use it to relax and treat my skin, and I’m incorporating getting massages, too, because I need to get better about recouping. But at home, it’s the simple things. I obviously love my bed, and I love a Salt & Stone candle — it’s one of my favorite things to have in my room.” Miller isn’t just dancing for hours a day — she’s doing so while wearing heels. “You’ve got to break your shoes in and get used to them,” she says. “I’ve honestly been doing good so far and wearing socks with them. I’m the type of person where wearing a new shoe sometimes almost stresses me out, unless it’s for the look. But in this case, I knew I had to get acquainted with them early.” One of her go-to ways to care for achy feet is by using a foot spa. “I’m bringing back the pedicure bath things that I was like, I haven’t seen this thing in 20 years,” she says. “But I got one on Amazon, and I would say it’s one of my best purchases of 2026.” As for Miller’s favorite thing to nosh on pre-, post- and during rehearsal? “Fruit — I don’t like eating a heavy meal beforehand,” she says. “I love Solely fruit jerky. I swear by it and it helps spike my blood sugar if I’m feeling a little bit eh. It’s healthy and really great on the go.” There’s always Celcius in her refrigerator too, a brand she recently worked with to launch its Spritz Vibe beverage. Miller immediately stocked her DWTS trailer with Nexxus hair care when she got access to it. She’s been working with the brand throughout the year, and says its products continuously fit into different aspects of her life. “With Dancing with the Stars, we’re going to be in several different types of hairstyles, so you really need something that’s going to withstand the test of time from the wee hours of the morning to at night when we’re live on TV,” says Miller. “We all know I’m a glam girl — I love my glam, and obviously I’m going to be focused on it. But when it comes down to it, I need reliable products that I know are going to hold me through so my attention is on my dancing entirely.” Her favorite Nexxus product is the Air Shape Workable Hold Texture Spray. “I like volume. I like big hair. I want to pull it out and make it even bigger,” says Miller. “I’m a texture girl. And obviously I need a firm hairspray to hold it all in place, too.” Why trust NBC Selected?
